As many as 300,000 people here work in the industry.
Lighting firecrackers is a highlight for families during holidays like Diwali, known as the Festival of Lights.
But they are wreaking havoc on India's environment too, shrouding the air in a toxic smog.
On the night of Diwali, levels of harmful fine particle pollution can nearly quadruple.
So are these dazzling light shows worth the risk?
And how are the workers at the heart of this $740 million business staying safe?
Balumani lives in the town of Sivakasi in India's Tamil Nadu state with her husband and daughters.
She works at a firecracker factory about nine miles away from her home.
This is one of Tamil Nadu's driest regions, so jobs in farming or agriculture are hard to find.
So people like Balumani rely on the firecracker industry to make ends meet.
- - For the past 10 years, feeding her family has meant returning to the same factory day after day, even if every day, she runs the risk of not returning home at all.
She and 60 others work at Tank Fireworks, one of the city's roughly 1,000 firecracker factories.
Women make up about 75% of the workforce.
Balumani has been working here since she was 22 years old.
Tank Fireworks told us shifts are typically eight hours long, but employees said they can work as many as 15 hours during the peak season.
Today, she's filling firecracker casings with gunpowder before compacting them with a wooden peg.
They're making a firecracker called the watermelon.
When lit, the tubes will create a shower of multicolored sparks.
Firecrackers contain different chemical mixtures depending on the desired display.
Gunpowder is typically made from potassium nitrate, carbon, and sulfur.
When the fuse is lit, potassium nitrate supplies oxygen that helps the carbon and sulfur burn rapidly.
Other chemicals can add color to the display.
Strontium makes red, copper makes blue, and aluminum makes silver.
Balumani has to make sure the tubes are evenly packed so each firecracker ignites in the same way.
Another worker, Sakthivel, wears only a disposable face mask for protection.
He's been making fireworks for almost three decades.
He says workers like him aren't allowed to wear footwear of any kind because debris from outside could increase the risk of fire.
- - Temperatures inside these workshops often exceed 100 degrees Fahrenheit, but air conditioning and fans generally aren't allowed in these workshops.
A single spark from a fan motor could cause a catastrophic explosion on contact with the gunpowder.
Each stage of production takes place inside its own small shed to prevent an accidental explosion from spreading throughout the factory.
Despite best efforts to contain risk, accidents still happen at factories throughout the region.
In 2012, at least 33 factory workers were killed while mixing chemicals for firecrackers.
- - Between 2019 and 2023, factory explosions in Tamil Nadu killed 131 people and left 146 others with critical injuries.
Explosions may be the most obvious threat here, but just breathing the air in these confined spaces can be a killer too.
Exposure to substances like sulfur, potassium nitrate, and aluminum powder can lead to long-term health problems including asthma, lung scarring, and chronic bronchitis.
Pressure to ramp up production can also increase the risk of accidents.
Legally, only four people are allowed to be in a work shed at any time, but that number can double in the weeks leading up to Diwali.
Indian authorities also set maximum limits on chemical storage and strictly regulate how raw materials are transported.
Firecracker making is still a very hands-on process.
Once the firecrackers are filled, they are sealed with glue or clay.
They're all laid out in the sun to dry for three to five hours.
Trapped moisture inside the casing can ruin the gunpowder.
The firecrackers are then individually wrapped, labeled and packed into colorful boxes.
They'll be shipped to retail shops like Tank Crackers, which is about three miles away.
- - At this store, Karthiga and her brother can sell 20 to 30 boxes of firecrackers per day and about 80 online.
The cheapest ones, typically noise makers, sell for about 30 rupees or 35 cents each.
Novelty firecrackers are much more expensive, 1,200 to 5,000 rupees or 12 to $50 a piece.
- - Factories in Sivakasi make about 50,000 tons of firecrackers every year.
In 2025, the industry brought in $740 million.
It's the backbone of the local economy.
- - The story of Sivakasi's firecracker industry began with the arrival of Japanese migrants to India in the 1910s, but they weren't making firecrackers back then, they were making matches.
A small number of factories started popping up in what was then Calcutta.
By the 1920s, the industry had spread to Sivakasi due to the pioneering efforts of two cousins.
The cottage industry quickly grew with workers learning about each stage of handmade match production.
Then during World War II, wartime restrictions curbed imports on firecrackers.
Matches and firecrackers used similar materials, so matchstick makers were well-placed to fill the void.
In the days before Diwali, millions of people in Delhi swarm local shops to prepare for the holiday.
- - Diwali symbolizes the victory of light over darkness.
The holiday falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar calendar, usually between mid-October and mid-November.
- - These days, no Diwali celebration is complete without firecrackers and sparklers.
- - But when the celebrations are over, another problem emerges.
Trash and discarded firecrackers litter the streets, much of it ending up in already polluted waterways.
And then there is this, a thick blanket of smog lingering over the city.

So when you were waking up, you know, those mornings in November, you saw complete smog, which was not happening before that.
- The air quality in Delhi deteriorates sharply in the days following Diwali, often reaching hazardous levels.
Around midnight after Diwali in 2025, harmful particle pollution in one part of the city hit 994 micrograms per cubic meter.
That's over 65 times the World Health Organization's guideline for a 24-hour average.
The smoke can aggravate asthma and other lung conditions, sending some people into respiratory distress.
- I've been shown that the night of Diwali, there is a 50 to 60% increase of respiratory admissions in the pediatric wards.
- Environmental activist Bhavreen Kandhari co-founded Warrior Moms, which advocates for clean air as a human right.
- It's heartbreaking to see how everybody is affected.
The people have a phobia of Diwali now.
- Delhi is already one of the most polluted cities in the world.
In 2016, India's Supreme Court temporarily barred stores in Delhi and nearby cities from selling firecrackers in an attempt to limit the pollution.
But the restrictions were difficult to enforce and threatened thousands of jobs in the firecracker industry.
Two years later, the court instead told manufacturers to shift to green firecrackers, which reportedly caused 20 to 30% less air pollution than traditional firecrackers.
So-called green firecrackers use fewer chemicals than traditional ones and contain additives like zeolite and iron oxide.
The additives bind with fine soot and dust, creating heavier compounds that settle on the ground rather than linger in the air.
Officials require green firecrackers to have a QR code that can be easily scanned to verify authenticity, but enforcing this law is hard.

On average, firecracker makers in Sivakasi earn only a few thousand rupees per week, roughly $30.
